I used to COVID has destroyed my list though. 😢 its okay we have a vaccine now 😛 Watching just about every country destroy itself due to fear has thrown a bit of a wrench in things. It isn't COVID specifically that I have a problem with. It is the willingness of governments to go against their own laws to satisfy mass fear, and the willingness of populations to accept that. I would never have thought that Switzerland would start mandating what people have to wear when going outside or restrict who can enter/leave the country or what businesses can operate, yet nearly overnight they did. hmm by that metric i guess america would be top Whether COVID was a real threat or not, I don't believe it is acceptable for a government to exercise such power without sufficient checks and balances. The US shutdown all international travel at a federal level IIRC, so not exactly a beacon of hope. Also, the US is off my list for many other reasons. 🙂 There are a number of states in the US I would happily move to if they seceded from the US though. 🙂 There are very few countries that *didn't* exercise what I consider to be insane government overreach without warning. And those few don't make my list of places to live for other reasons. As an example, I believe Belarus didn't exercise any crazy governmental powers, but it is also a communist country IIRC, which I'm not interested in as someone who has machinations of starting a business. Singapore is strange... I increasingly get the impression that the government is significantly more pro-freedom than the people (!!) Of course, if every country was nearly equally bad, I could just ignore the whole COVID thing and accept it as part of what it means to exist within modern society. 🙂 Really? Why is that? Not that I disagree, Singapore *generally* has a track record at the state level of being pretty pro freedom, while the people (especially native born Singaporeans) increasingly appear to be demanding more and more government oversight. However, having not lived there I'm curious to hear about your personal experiences. Here's a very recent example of what I mean https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/opinion/article/3111498/travel-bubble-what-singapore-and-hong-kongs-contrasting-reactions > In Singapore, many people responded to the suspension of the travel bubble with a mix of barely concealed glee and a smug “I told you so”, blaming transport minister Ong Ye Kung for lacking the foresight to anticipate what should have been obvious: that quarantine-free travel between the city state and Hong Kong was a bad idea that should not have been contemplated in the first place. > > In reality, it was quite brave of the transport minister to pursue the idea. If he had not negotiated a travel bubble, and we subsequently found out that the rise in cases over the following months was minimal and manageable, he would not be blamed for lacking the vision and appetite for risk to take advantage of the opportunity. Another example of this is immigration politics; Singapore is historically super-immigrant-oriented (>1/3 of population foreign born), but recently they've been constricting a bit, and it's definitely pressure from the local public that's causing it My theory is that most people don't understand where their prosperity comes from. Philippines is a great example of this with their cargo cult mentality. They see the US as prosperous, so they mimic what the US does. However, the set of things they mimic are not the things that made the US prosperous, so they end up often times worse off than if they just ignored the US entirely. This, sadly, makes me a bit nervous about the future of Singapore. Nationalism is incredibly enticing and very popular in the world today, but I (personally) believe that it is really bad for prosperity. SG definitely has a strong globalist ethos even despite all this; I remember getting into a taxi where the taxi driver asked me and a friend where we're from, and when I asked him the same question he replied "we're all human" Parts of the US do as well, but it feels like it's really been declining in the last ~5 years Countries by immigrant population: United Arab Emirates: 87.9 Qatar: 78.7 Kuwait: 72.1 British Virgin Islands: 69.2 Monaco: 68.0 Liechtenstein: 67.0 Sint Maarten (Dutch part): 66.7 Turks and Caicos Islands: 64.2 China, Macao SAR: 62.4 Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba: 59.6 Maybe that should be my starter list. 😬 As a proxy for "countries that aren't terribly nationalistic". Yep, the Gulf states are basically small elites with a lot of money that just hire a labor force I should really visit one or more gulf states one of these days (more than just an airport). I have no idea what life is *actually* like there. Having spent a total of nearly a year in SG and still knowing almost nothing about the migrant worker community, I do think it's important to keep in mind the limits of what you'll learn 😆 Do you feel like you have a good grasp on the long term trajectory of Singapore? hmm If I had to guess, I would say "partial regression-to-the-mean but still quite positive for the next few decades" 🤔 I suspect my problem is that I'm trying to see too far into the future. Digital Nomads only try to see 3-6 months into the future, while I'm here trying to plan for 100 years... which is pure folly. My least favorite thing about Singapore is that the culture is clearly very materialistic and money-oriented. It's easy to see from the youtube ads you get here: "do YOU want to earn a SECOND INCOME, by passively sitting on some investments?" There's little "do cool stuff for the sake of doing cool stuff" I was thinking about starting a physical business, which would require buying land, developing it, investing in machinery, etc. all of which is not particularly mobile.
